Now, about the hot-dog/sausage thing:

A hot-dog is not a sausage in Polish. We make a clear distinction between parówki (hot-dogs) and kiełbasy (sausages): a Pole would never call a parówka a kiełbasa, and vice versa.

Hot-dogs are made cheaply from lowest quality ingredients: fat, nearly worthless offcuts, and mechanically separated meat scraps, with copious amounts of industrial additives, all ground into a pulp. It's no wonder that the Polish expression for the contents of parówka is "pies zmielony razem z budą" - dog minced together with the doghouse. Parówka is by definition ultra-highly processed. All parówki look and taste almost the same.

Kiełbasa is made from high quality meat, with actual meat chunks still present and recognizable in the end product. It is a processed product, sure, but not an ultra-high processed one. Many Polish kiełbasy are made artisanally by local producers, and they came in countless types, differentiated by girth, the type of meat used, spices and herbs added, whether they were smoked or not, etc. The appearance and taste of different kiełbasy may vary greatly.

Is there anyone who doesn't love Rigel?

I mean, there it is.  Right in the Beverly Hills of the constellations, Orion, the intrepid hunter with the diamond belt.  And it's not just a part of the constellation--Rigel and Betelgeuse are the Richard Burton/Elizabeth Taylor of celestial sphere.

They are both giants.  In fact, about the only stars we see in the sky are giants.  Anything as mediocre as our sun can hardly be discerned at more than 20-40 lightyears, and so there are only a few hundred stars out there that could actually see us if their alien eyes were like our eyes.   Very little chance we are some other star's Rigel.

Rigel is roughly a basketball to our sun as a fly (a spherical fly--work with me here).  And Betelgeuse oscillates around 10 times larger than *that*.  I say oscillates, because Betelgeuse displays a scary instability, and can grow and shrink by nearly a factor of two over the course of 13 earth months.

In fact, Betelgeuse is acting so strangely there's a thought that it'll go supernova in the near future--say the next few hundreds of thousands of years.  A supernova as near to us as Betelgeuse (a few hundred lightyears) would be very, very exciting.

So anyway, the Rigel/Betelgeuse glamor couple anchoring a most gorgeous constellation is well worth seeing.  But not just yet.  It will be peaking out ahead of the sun about this time of year, and will gradually get more and more prominent as we go through autumn and winter.

It's really nifty to come up with four such strong and in-the-language theme answers based on the repurposing of ordinary computer-related words.  I loved this puzzle -- much more than I ordinarily love Tuesday offerings.  I also loved the wry, tongue-in-cheek way the "https" clues were written.  "Hot-dog.org".  Wonderful!!

The "computer words" SITE, LINK and ADDRESS came to me immediately once I had most of  the first words.  The exception was SENATE PAGE, which is delightful wordplay.  

In fact, it would have been a perfect puzzle had it not been for one entry that I am happy to say I didn't know.  
Did I not know PANTSED because of my gender or my generation?  Not sure.  Women didn't wear pants back in the day, so we couldn't have been PANTSED back then.  But we do wear pants now, so now we can be.  ARE we?  I have no idea.  But I like to think we're not, because girls are so much more mature than boys and we wouldn't waste our time on such puerile nonsense.  And if a boy were to do it to a girl, then it wouldn't be PANTSing -- it would be something entirely different...and actionable.

Question of the day: Is there such a thing as a PANT SET?  PANT SET/TELL would be so much nicer a pair of answers.  But I sort of don't think there is such a thing.  Pity.

Still, a delightful theme, beautifully executed and much fun to solve.

So, I was thinking about non-linearity effects in puzzle solving time, which perhaps is the most obvious thought process ever, but maybe not?

I struggled on Friday, getting a foothold here and there and eventually looked up the soccer star to put myself out of my misery. It took me about 55 minutes. I probably could have puzzled it out, but my time would be well over an hour. XW stats rated it "hard"

Saturday was house on fire, and I finished in 23 minutes, more than an hour faster than my average. (note my averages are hideous... but still an HOUR faster!) XW stats rated it "average"

For the Sat. puzzle, I was filling in big chunks at a time, which meant I had a huge advantage on getting the crosses right... everything fell like dominoes.

I was thinking about all the speedy solvers, and regulars, and smart math people in this forum @francis @sp @B ... do you guys ever think about this? 

Like some sort of quadratic effect ... getting X number of words close to each other in the grid leads to improving one's time Y-fold... Or: "If I know with certainty Z number of words and they are in a certain neighborhood of each other, my time will improve Z-fold?" I guess what I am saying that that knowing some answers with certainty matters (skill), as does how close those answers end up near each other in the grid (maybe this is a luck factor)?

Anyway, feel free to go do some math!

@Niki B

I think you are spot on.  

The worst is when a pass yields answers, but no answer provides more than one letter for the remaining unknowns.  

Much better to have the same number of answers, but grouped so that they provide two or more letters for the crosses.  

My feeling is that, *for the average word*, the chances are much better of finding a remaining unknowns increases faster than linear, probably exponentially.  This works best for words and phrases, less so for proper names. 

So, for example, having four letters of an eight letter answer is better than twice a good as if we only had two letters.

Of course, exceptions are not rare--we've all experienced having a single space and cannot for the life of us figure out which of the 26 letters (ignoring rebuses) is the right one.

I would love to be able to actually do the math, but I fear it's beyond me (so far!).  

I would really love if the app were able to replay the solve from start to finish, including how much thinking time there is between correct entries.  Then one could actually start to plug in actual values for actual situations.  Over a large number of puzzles I think a pattern of sorts would start to emerge.

@Niki B

Thinking a little more about it...

Suppose we have a completely random set of letters, and an answer with six letters (ignoring rebuses).

There is a 26^6 (26x26x26x26x26x26) utterly naive guesses.

So we have only one chance in roughly 300 million of guessing it right.  

If we have one cross, that leaves only 26^5 possibilities of the remaining letters--we're 26 times more likely to guess the remaining five.

That's fairly straightforward.  But for better or worse, our chance of guessing are much higher than one in 26^6 because we have some notion of what is right and letter sequences are surely wrong.  So the probabilities are some unknown x^6, and each additional cross increases our chances by x.

Problem is, x is not a fixed number--it'll vary for different people and different answers.  But there *might* be some average x.  

If I ever come up with a reasonable estimate for an average x, you can be sure I'll post it.

@Francis

I like the toe hold you created by imagining that a person could randomly (blindly) guess at each of the letters in an answer.

This leads to the observation that there are a variety of approaches to solving and a variety of factors that affect difficulty.

For example, a moderately skilled solver knows that certain letters go together more often than others, M and P, N and D, Q and U, etc. I doubt there are many words where an N precedes a P or an I follows a Q. This helps to limit the possible letters for some squares.

Also, some names are more likely in American English than others, so with a couple of letters of an unknown celebrity, it is often easier to suss out the other letters.

So I would say that a person's understanding of linguistic and cultural norms along with the particular letters that have been "revealed" will interact to adjust difficulty. And of course, knowledge of trivia, that hated information that you know but I do not.

And as you once pointed out, I believe, a couple of "gimmes" in the right places can make a puzzle much, much easier.
